title: Javascript Variables
summary: Introduces variables as named containers for data, using var. Shows prompt() for user input, why unsaved input is lost, reassigning a variable, using a variable inside alert, and combining strings and variables with +.

concepts.heading: Why variables
points: A variable stores a value in the computer's memory under a name so it can be reused without retyping or re-asking for it.
Without storing, data from a prompt is gone as soon as the dialog closes.

concepts.heading: prompt()
points: prompt("What is your name?"); looks like alert but also shows a text field. The user types text and clicks OK.
The call evaluates to the entered text (a string), so it can be assigned to a variable. (Extra) Cancel returns null, and numbers typed in still arrive as strings.
Run a snippet with Cmd/Ctrl+Enter or the run button in Chrome DevTools > Sources > Snippets.

concepts.heading: Declaring and assigning with var
points: Syntax: var myName = "Angela"; The keyword var creates a new container, myName is its label, = places the value on the right into it, and the semicolon ends the statement.
After running the snippet, typing myName in the Console returns the stored string, proving it stays in memory.
Reassign by writing the name alone: myName = "Jimmy"; The old value is replaced. Do not repeat var; it is used only once, when the variable is first created.
Referring to a variable (no quotes) retrieves its value. alert(myName); shows the value; alert("myName"); would show the literal word.
(Extra) The course uses var here; modern code prefers let and const (the playground teaches those). var is function-scoped and can be redeclared, which causes bugs.

concepts.heading: Combining text and variables
points: The + operator joins strings and variable values into one message: alert("My name is " + myName + ", welcome to my course " + yourName + "!");
Spaces and punctuation must be placed inside the quoted pieces, because + adds nothing between them.
Variables hold changing state: a gameLevel variable can start at 1, be updated to 2 and 3 as the player progresses, and be shown with alert("Your level is currently: " + gameLevel);.

pitfalls: Putting quotes around the variable name, which prints the name instead of its value.
Repeating var when you only want to change the value.
Missing spaces inside concatenated strings, so words run together.
Calling prompt() without assigning it, so the input is lost.
